old: you will not find us fail you
new: you will not find us failing you
reason: Current English does not take a bare infinitive after 'find' + object in this sense. It says 'find us failing you'. So Telemachus's promise of loyalty reads as a dropped '-ing', a typo rather than a dated idiom, on the page and aloud. PUNCTUATION.md §5 (D16) repairs Butler's marks on the same test: fix what a modern reader takes for an error. Butler's verb, object and sense are kept, and only the verb form changes. The meaning is recoverable, so this is optional. Nothing else in ¶12 moves, including 'Look to it yourself', which is ruled on separately and kept.

old: Bring the bed outside this room
new: Bring the bed outside that room
reason: This is a deixis problem. Butler's 'this' points back to the chamber named in the sentence before, which Victorian prose allowed. In present-day speech, 'this room' means the room the speaker is standing in. Penelope is speaking in the hall (¶8: the fire, the pillars, the seat opposite Odysseus). So her second order seems to send the bed out of the hall, and the two orders appear to contradict each other at the trap the scene turns on. 'that' sends the reader back to the bedroom, as Butler's 'this' does, and the Greek has 'there' (ἔνθα) at this point. One word changes. Nothing is added or resolved: the order is still the trick that ¶17 exposes. The accepted ¶16 wording ('put on airs', 'belittle') is untouched.

old: had had enough both of his wife and of rest
new: had had his fill both of his wife and of rest
reason: The modernization introduced this false friend. Butler has no 'enough'. His elliptical 'had had both of his wife and of repose' means Odysseus had taken his pleasure of both. With a person as its object, 'have had enough of' is the current idiom for being fed up ('I've had enough of you'). So, at the close of the reunion, the line now says Athena judged Odysseus tired of Penelope. The drafter supplied 'enough' to Butler's elliptical 'had had', as the edition does harmlessly at 8.44 ('had had to eat and drink' becomes 'had had enough to eat and drink'). With food as the object, 'enough' means satisfied, as in Butler's own 'had had enough to eat and drink' (3.7, 4.7, 8.5); with a person as the object, it means fed up. 'his fill' is Butler's own word for the same enjoyment two paragraphs earlier: 'When Ulysses and Penelope had had their fill of love' (¶25, printed so in the modern). It renders the same Greek verb (τέρπομαι: εὐνῆς ἧς ἀλόχου ταρπήμεναι ἠδὲ καὶ ὕπνου), and the echo steers the reading. 'both … and', 'wife' and 'rest' stay.

old: it will at once get abroad
new: it will at once get about
reason: This is a dead sense. 'abroad' now means 'overseas', and 'get abroad' for 'become known' has dropped out of use, so the reader had to rule out 'go overseas'. The same Book already prints Butler's own phrase for the same event, the news of the killing spreading through the town: 'no rumors about the suitors' death will get about in the town' (¶13). Using it here restores Butler's phrase under D29 rather than inventing a new rendering, and 24.28 already renders Butler's 'noised abroad' as 'spread news of'. One word changes. The 'that' clause makes the meaning recoverable, so this is optional.
